items.question: Which factor is MOST important to quantify when projecting monthly API costs for a new Claude integration?

options.A: The average token volume per API call multiplied by the number of calls per day
options.B: The number of employees who will have access to the integration
options.C: The geographic region where the API requests will be processed
options.D: The number of documents stored in the Project knowledge base

items.question: A business owner is reviewing a new Claude API integration with a developer. Which API-level parameter gives the developer the ability to set consistent, application-wide instructions?

options.A: Temperature — a sampling parameter that controls output randomness
options.B: The system prompt — a pre-conversation instruction layer set by the developer that applies to every user session
options.C: The context window — the total token capacity available per session
options.D: The API key — the authentication credential that authorises the integration to make calls

items.question: Which capability is NECESSARY for an agent to take real-world actions such as querying a database or submitting a form?

options.A: Extended reasoning, which gives the model additional internal steps before responding
options.B: A multi-tier model pipeline that routes complex subtasks to a higher-tier model
options.C: Tool use (function calling), which allows the model to invoke external systems during a response
options.D: A fine-tuned model trained on examples of the specific system's interaction format

items.question: A team wants to validate that their RAG system consistently returns correct answers from the document corpus. Which approach gives the MOST meaningful quality signal?

options.A: Confirming that the retrieval step returns results within an acceptable latency threshold
options.B: Counting how many API calls complete without rate-limit errors per hour
options.C: Measuring the percentage of responses that exceed a minimum word count
options.D: Creating a test set of questions with known correct answers and comparing the system's responses against them

items.question: When should a team escalate from prompt engineering to fine-tuning?

options.A: When the desired behaviour cannot be achieved reliably through prompting and representative examples, even after thorough iteration
options.B: When Claude consistently produces outputs that are too long despite explicit length constraints in the prompt
options.C: When the team wants to reduce per-call token cost by removing context from the prompt
options.D: When the team wants to gain access to a newer base model that is only available through fine-tuning

items.question: A developer is evaluating whether to use Claude Code or call the Claude API directly for an automated code review pipeline. What is the PRIMARY advantage Claude Code offers for this use case?

options.A: Claude Code uses a lower-tier model by default, reducing cost for automated pipelines
options.B: Claude Code can navigate the repository's file structure, read multiple files, and run tests locally without the developer writing custom integration code for those operations
options.C: Claude Code has higher rate limits than the standard API for automated code workflows
options.D: Claude Code includes a built-in eval framework that scores code quality without configuration

items.question: Which TWO controls are BOTH required for comprehensive access governance when an organisation has employees using Claude and also builds Claude-powered applications? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Fine-tuning the model on proprietary style to reduce out-of-policy responses
options.B: SSO integration to govern employee access through the corporate identity provider
options.C: Prompt caching to reduce the cost of frequently reused system prompts
options.D: API key management with rotation and minimum-scope access for applications that call Claude programmatically
options.E: Batch processing for all application calls to reduce cost and avoid rate limits

items.question: A team runs a nightly job processing thousands of support tickets, each requiring a lookup in a document corpus. Which architecture MOST efficiently handles this workload?

options.A: Synchronous API calls that include the entire document corpus in the context window for each ticket
options.B: A fine-tuned model with the document corpus embedded in its weights, avoiding retrieval at runtime
options.C: Batch processing combined with retrieval — each ticket triggers a retrieval step to fetch relevant passages, then the batch queue processes all ticket-passage pairs asynchronously
options.D: A separate agent per ticket running concurrently to process all tickets simultaneously

items.question: A team is designing a pipeline that will process 50,000 documents per day through the Claude API. When should rate limits PRIMARILY influence the architectural design?

options.A: Only after the pipeline is deployed and call failures are observed in production
options.B: Only when using the highest-tier model, which has more restrictive rate limits than lower tiers
options.C: Only when the pipeline includes real-time user-facing responses, not automated background processing
options.D: During the initial design phase, so the pipeline includes queuing and pacing mechanisms that prevent the throughput from exceeding allowed limits from day one

items.question: After enabling prompt caching on a long system prompt, a team wants to confirm that caching has not changed output quality. What is the MOST appropriate approach?

options.A: Run the same eval test set against the cached and uncached configurations and compare the quality scores
options.B: Monitor the response length distribution, as quality changes from caching produce longer or shorter responses
options.C: Check that the API returns a 'cache hit' status on every call, confirming the cache is operating correctly
options.D: Compare the per-call token count before and after caching — unchanged token counts confirm quality is unchanged

items.question: Which TWO task characteristics MOST strongly indicate that the highest-tier model is the right choice rather than the mid-tier? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The task requires synthesising ambiguous evidence from multiple sources to make a nuanced judgement
options.B: The task involves classifying 10,000 records using a well-defined, consistent label taxonomy
options.C: The task involves multi-step reasoning where an early wrong inference would propagate into an incorrect final analysis
options.D: The task is extracting structured fields from a standard-format document with clear, repeating patterns
options.E: The task requires generating a first-draft email from a brief set of bullet points

items.question: In an agentic workflow that can send emails and update customer records, when should a human approval checkpoint be placed?

options.A: After every tool call, so no action is taken without human review
options.B: Before any irreversible action is executed, so a human can confirm correctness before the action takes effect
options.C: Only when the agent encounters an error, as a human fallback handler
options.D: At the end of the entire workflow, as a final review before delivery

items.question: What is the correct relationship between model version pinning and a formal eval programme?

options.A: Pinning eliminates the need for evals because the model behaviour is fixed and cannot change
options.B: Evals eliminate the need for pinning because quality is continuously measured and alerts fire when it degrades
options.C: Pinning ensures evals measure a stable baseline; evals then detect whether an intentional model upgrade maintains the required quality before the team migrates
options.D: Evals determine which model version the team should pin by scoring all available versions simultaneously

items.question: A pipeline processing very long documents stops mid-analysis because the maximum output length is reached before the analysis is complete. What is the MOST appropriate architectural response?

options.A: Switch to batch processing, which offers higher output length limits for asynchronous jobs
options.B: Increase the temperature setting to allow the model to generate longer sequences before terminating
options.C: Reduce the number of retrieved passages sent per call to free up token space for the output
options.D: Segment the document into smaller sections, process each independently, and aggregate the outputs to stay within per-call output limits

items.question: A developer uses Claude Code to automate code review by pulling external package documentation from the web. What prompt injection risk does this introduce?

options.A: External documentation pages could contain hidden instructions attempting to alter Claude Code's review behaviour or cause it to execute unintended commands on the local machine
options.B: External documentation may contain copyrighted code samples that Claude Code would incorporate directly into the reviewed codebase
options.C: Web documentation retrieval increases latency to a level that triggers rate limit errors during the review
options.D: External documentation pages are typically too large for Claude Code's context window, preventing the review from completing

items.question: An organisation runs two workflows: high-volume email classification (10,000 emails per day) and low-volume complex contract analysis (50 documents per week). Which tier strategy MOST efficiently balances cost and quality?

options.A: Use the highest-tier model for both workflows to ensure consistent quality across the organisation
options.B: Use a lower-tier model for the high-volume classification and the highest tier for the complex contract analysis
options.C: Use batch processing for both workflows regardless of tier to lower cost across the board
options.D: Fine-tune a single mid-tier model for both workflows to avoid maintaining multiple configurations

items.question: After fine-tuning a model on domain-specific examples, a team's eval programme should include which test category that was NOT necessary before fine-tuning?

options.A: Rate limit stress tests to confirm the fine-tuned model handles production throughput
options.B: Temperature sensitivity tests to verify the fine-tuned model responds consistently at all temperature values
options.C: General-capability tests on tasks NOT included in the fine-tuning data, to detect potential catastrophic forgetting
options.D: Context window tests to confirm that fine-tuning has not altered the maximum input capacity

items.question: Which TWO conditions TOGETHER represent the strongest case for migrating a use case from Claude.ai chat to an API integration? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The team wants to consolidate all Claude interactions into one interface for audit purposes
options.B: The use case requires embedding Claude in a product where end users interact through a custom interface, not Claude.ai directly
options.C: The team's prompt has grown longer than comfortably fits in a single chat message
options.D: The workflow processes hundreds of consistent, structured requests per day with results fed automatically into a downstream system
options.E: The team wants to use Artifacts for richer formatted outputs

items.question: How do rate limits affect agentic workflows differently from simple single-call pipelines?

options.A: Rate limits only apply to synchronous calls; agentic workflows using batch processing are completely exempt
options.B: Rate limits prevent agents from using tools, as tool calls do not count against the standard API rate limits
options.C: Rate limits are automatically relaxed for agentic workflows to accommodate their higher call volumes
options.D: Each model call and tool call within an agent task consumes rate limit capacity, meaning one complex agentic task can exhaust the rate limit many times faster than a single-call approach

items.question: Which TWO elements must a business professional provide to a developer to enable a successful Claude API integration — items the developer cannot substitute from technical documentation alone? (Choose TWO)

options.A: A clear specification of what Claude should and should not do, including scope, tone, and behavioural constraints
options.B: The exact API endpoint URL and authentication header format the developer should use
options.C: A description of what good output looks like, ideally with examples or a scoring rubric the developer can use in testing
options.D: The names of the SDK libraries and the programming language the development team prefers
options.E: A list of third-party libraries that are compatible with the Anthropic SDK

items.question: What symptom most directly indicates that the prompt is missing background context the model cannot infer?

options.A: The output is longer than the user requested
options.B: The output is generic and could apply to any situation rather than the specific one described
options.C: The output is in the wrong structural format
options.D: The model declines to complete the task

items.question: Which prompt element, when absent, most commonly causes Claude to produce output in the wrong structure or format?

options.A: A role instruction specifying an area of expertise
options.B: Background context about the organisation or situation
options.C: A chain-of-thought directive asking the model to reason step by step
options.D: An explicit format specification describing the desired output structure

items.question: What is the primary cause when Claude produces output that is shorter than needed and stops before covering all required points?

options.A: No length or depth instruction was provided in the prompt
options.B: The model tier selected was below the complexity of the task
options.C: The context window was saturated by prior turns in the conversation
options.D: The task was spread across too many separate prompt turns

items.question: Claude consistently produces formal, technical prose when the intended audience is non-specialist readers. Which missing prompt element is MOST likely responsible?

options.A: A format specification describing the desired output structure
options.B: A constraint on the maximum length of the response
options.C: An audience or tone instruction identifying who the output is for
options.D: A chain-of-thought directive asking the model to reason before responding

items.question: Claude's output addresses a different question than the one intended. Which diagnostic step should come FIRST?

options.A: Switch to a higher model tier to improve comprehension
options.B: Re-read the prompt for ambiguous phrasing or asks buried late in the text
options.C: Add few-shot examples showing the desired answer type
options.D: Decompose the prompt into a sequence of smaller prompts

items.question: Claude returns an overly cautious refusal on a clearly legitimate professional request. Which intervention is MOST targeted?

options.A: Switch to Opus, which applies a higher threshold before refusing
options.B: Rephrase the request as a hypothetical scenario to avoid triggering safety checks
options.C: Add more detail to the task description itself
options.D: Add context that establishes the legitimate professional purpose for the request

items.question: Across repeated runs of an identical prompt, Claude produces notably different outputs each time. What does this symptom most directly suggest?

options.A: The prompt lacks sufficient specificity to constrain the output space to a narrow range
options.B: The model tier is inappropriate for a task that requires consistent results
options.C: The context window is being truncated between runs, altering what the model sees
options.D: The task is inherently a poor fit for Claude and should be handled differently

items.question: Claude gives shallow analysis on a complex topic. Which distinction determines whether adding context or upgrading the model tier is the correct fix?

options.A: Whether the output is shorter than a specified length target
options.B: Whether the current model is Haiku, because Haiku always requires upgrading for analytical tasks
options.C: Whether the prompt supplied adequate background — if not, adding context should come before any tier change
options.D: Whether the user has already reformulated the prompt at least once without improvement

items.question: What is the recommended approach when Claude's output is cut off mid-response and the complete answer does not fit one turn?

options.A: Re-send the entire original prompt with an instruction to write a longer response
options.B: Ask Claude to continue from where it stopped, or request the remaining section explicitly
options.C: Upgrade to a model with a larger context window to prevent truncation
options.D: Redesign the task as a sequence of smaller prompts from the beginning

items.question: What is the primary signal that it is time to start a new conversation rather than continuing the current one?

options.A: The user has sent more than ten messages in the current thread
options.B: Claude begins producing output in the wrong structural format
options.C: The context window usage indicator shows that the conversation is long
options.D: Responses begin drifting off-topic or contradicting accurate statements made earlier in the thread

items.question: When critical content is buried in the middle of a long document passed as context, what is the most reliable corrective technique?

options.A: Move the critical material closer to the start or end of the document, or reference it explicitly in the prompt
options.B: Switch to a higher model tier that is better at retrieving mid-document content
options.C: Split the document into multiple uploads across separate conversation turns
options.D: Ask Claude to summarise the entire document before posing the question

items.question: What is the correct distinction between output that is *truncated* and output that is *refused*?

options.A: Truncated output contains an explicit error message; refused output simply ends without warning
options.B: Truncation occurs only in API calls; refusals occur only in chat interfaces
options.C: Truncated output stops before completing a valid response; a refusal is an explicit statement that the task will not be performed
options.D: Truncated output is caused by prompt length; refusals are caused by content policy detection in the system prompt

items.question: A prompt that worked well previously now produces poor results when run in the same conversation. Which variable should be isolated first?

options.A: Whether the model tier has been changed since the earlier run
options.B: Whether conversation context has accumulated differently — test the prompt in a fresh chat
options.C: Whether the task has grown beyond the model's current capability level
options.D: Whether Anthropic has updated the underlying model since the last successful run

items.question: When debugging a prompt that produces unsatisfactory output, why is it important to change only one element at a time?

options.A: The context window is consumed faster when multiple prompt elements change simultaneously
options.B: Changing multiple elements simultaneously risks triggering a content policy response
options.C: The model's sampling temperature interacts unpredictably with simultaneous prompt changes
options.D: Simultaneous changes make it impossible to identify which specific change caused any observed improvement

items.question: Project-level custom instructions specify a formal tone. The user's per-chat prompt requests a casual, conversational style. What determines Claude's behaviour?

options.A: Claude typically gives precedence to Project instructions because they function at a higher level than per-chat prompts, but the specific interaction should be tested
options.B: Project instructions always override per-chat prompts without exception, regardless of specificity
options.C: Per-chat prompts always override Project instructions because they represent the user's most recent intent
options.D: Claude produces output in both styles and asks the user to select the preferred version

items.question: Which combination of signals most accurately identifies a cost optimisation opportunity rather than a quality problem?

options.A: Outputs are inconsistent across runs and sometimes omit required sections
options.B: The model frequently refuses requests that are clearly within the intended scope
options.C: Output quality consistently meets requirements but the model tier in use is above what the task complexity warrants
options.D: Responses take longer than expected and output quality is acceptable but not excellent

items.question: Which TWO of the following symptoms indicate that the prompt is missing a *constraint*, rather than missing *context*? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The output is factually vague because the model lacks domain-specific background
options.B: The output includes material the user explicitly did not want included
options.C: The output is in the wrong language
options.D: The output is longer than needed and includes irrelevant elaboration
options.E: The model declines to answer on the grounds that the request is ambiguous

items.question: Which TWO of the following are causes of *conversation drift* rather than causes of a single-turn output failure? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Important early instructions being progressively diluted by a large volume of subsequent turns
options.B: The task description being too vague from the first message in the conversation
options.C: The model attending less reliably to constraints established early in the thread as the conversation grows
options.D: A format specification being absent from the original prompt
options.E: Using a model tier below the complexity of the task

items.question: Which TWO of the following interventions directly and reliably address output that is correct in content but wrong in format? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Provide few-shot examples of the correct reasoning process used to arrive at the answer
options.B: Add an explicit format specification to the prompt describing the required output structure
options.C: Switch to a higher model tier with stronger instruction-following capability
options.D: Include a concrete example of the exact output format expected
options.E: Increase the specificity of the task description

items.question: Which TWO conditions must both be true before escalating to a higher model tier is a justified troubleshooting step? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The prompt has already been revised to supply adequate context, constraints, and format guidance
options.B: The current model tier is Haiku, because escalation is only valid from the lowest tier
options.C: Output still fails to meet requirements after prompt improvement
options.D: The task involves multi-step reasoning rather than information retrieval or classification
options.E: The failure mode is incorrect output rather than a refusal

items.question: What is the term for the progressive degradation of output quality that occurs specifically as a conversation grows longer?

options.A: Conversation drift
options.B: Context truncation
options.C: Prompt decay
options.D: Output variance

items.question: Which of the following is the clearest signal that a task should NOT be automated with Claude?

options.A: The task requires reading a 50-page document and producing a structured summary
options.B: The task requires generating consistent formatted output at high volume
options.C: The task requires a legally binding determination that cannot be delegated away from a licensed professional
options.D: The task requires classifying incoming requests into predefined categories

items.question: What distinguishes a *prompt problem* from a *task fit problem* when troubleshooting poor output?

options.A: Prompt problems always produce shorter output than task fit problems
options.B: A prompt problem can be fixed by modifying the prompt; a task fit problem persists regardless of how the prompt is improved
options.C: Task fit problems arise only with lower model tiers; prompt problems arise across all tiers
options.D: A prompt problem causes refusals; a task fit problem produces incorrect output

items.question: When should a user escalate a persistent quality problem to IT or technical support rather than continuing to iterate on the prompt?

options.A: After more than three prompt iterations have failed to produce improvement
options.B: When output is consistently too short despite explicit length instructions
options.C: When the model tier is already Opus and output still falls short of requirements
options.D: When the symptoms suggest a configuration issue — such as unexpected system prompt behaviour, API integration errors, or rate limiting — that is outside the prompt itself

items.question: What is the primary purpose of capturing and documenting a prompt that produced high-quality output?

options.A: To enable consistent reuse across sessions and provide a baseline for future refinement or team adoption
options.B: To provide evidence of model capability for internal procurement justification
options.C: To protect the intellectual property embedded in the prompt's structure
options.D: To fine-tune a custom model version on proven examples

items.question: What is the correct distinction between an *instruction conflict* and an *instruction absence*?

options.A: An instruction conflict produces a refusal; an instruction absence produces generic output
options.B: Instruction conflicts occur only between Project and per-chat instructions; instruction absences occur within a single prompt
options.C: An instruction conflict means two present instructions impose incompatible requirements; an instruction absence means a required element was never specified
options.D: An instruction absence causes more severe output failures than an instruction conflict

items.question: What is the most reliable way to address conversation drift while preserving useful output already produced in the current thread?

options.A: Delete the earlier turns and re-run from the current point in the conversation
options.B: Start a fresh conversation and paste the relevant prior output as reference material in the new thread
options.C: Ask Claude to disregard its earlier responses and attend only to the most recent message
options.D: Upgrade to a higher model tier, which handles long conversation contexts more reliably

items.question: A workflow uses the highest model tier for a high-volume classification task. Output quality is good but costs are high. Which approach is correct?

options.A: Accept the current cost — the highest tier is required for any classification task to be reliable at volume
options.B: Downgrade to the lowest tier immediately, as classification tasks never require the highest tier
options.C: Add more constraints to the prompt so the model produces shorter responses, reducing token cost
options.D: Test whether the mid or lowest tier meets the quality requirement for this specific classification task, then use the lowest tier that passes

items.question: What does optimising for *latency* mean in a Claude workflow, and what is the primary trade-off?

options.A: Choosing a faster model tier or shorter prompt to reduce time-to-response, at potential cost to output depth or quality
options.B: Reducing the number of API calls by combining tasks into a single longer prompt
options.C: Using asynchronous batch processing to return results to the user sooner
options.D: Switching to cached context to eliminate repeated input processing overhead

items.question: What is the correct relationship between *context window* and *output length* as limiting factors in a Claude call?

options.A: They are the same limit — the context window governs both input and output as a single combined token budget
options.B: Output length limits only apply when the total context window is nearly full
options.C: They are independent limits — context window governs how much the model can receive; output length governs how long a single response can be
options.D: Context window is a constraint only in API calls; output length applies in both API and chat interfaces
